c.tagline: Spice-scented alleys where the Swahili coast meets the Indian Ocean.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree on the fare (often quoted in USD) before departing. Short in-town rides typically run $5-10.

emergency.note: Response times can be slow; many hotels/tour operators keep direct lines to private clinics like ZanMed or Mnazi Mmoja Hospital for serious cases.

hood_landmark.Stone Town (Mji Mkongwe): Stone Town Old Fort, Zanzibar City

avoid.reason: Avoid Stone Town's dark, deserted alleys and the beaches after nightfall, where bag-snatching and muggings occur.
Expect persistent 'papasi' touts around the port and Forodhani Gardens, and dress modestly, especially during Ramadan.

hood_desc: The UNESCO World Heritage core of winding alleys, carved wooden doors, bazaars, and rooftop restaurants; best for first-time visitors who want history, culture, and walkability.
A quieter, more residential extension of Stone Town along the seafront with guesthouses and mid-range hotels; good for travelers who want proximity to the old town without the busiest lanes.
A working harbor and market district on the edge of Stone Town, gritty and authentic with the famous Darajani Market; suits budget travelers and those wanting a local, non-touristy base.

water.note: Unreliable water distribution and infrastructure make tap water unsafe; drink bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: Dala-dala fares are paid in cash (small TZS notes) directly to the conductor on board; no card or app payment exists. Taxis and ride-hail (Little app) are paid in cash or via the app respectively. Ferries to Dar es Salaam are booked and paid for at the port ticket offices or through operators like Azam Marine.
transit.hours: Dala-dalas run roughly 6am-8pm with limited service after dark; taxis and the Little app operate 24 hours.
transit.note: Zanzibar City itself has no formal metro/tram; most visitors walk Stone Town and use taxis, tuk-tuks, or rented scooters for longer trips.

bus: Long-distance buses to other parts of Unguja island from Darajani terminal
ferry: Kilimanjaro Fast Ferries (to Dar es Salaam and Pemba)

transit.m: Dala-dala (shared minibus) to Stone Town, ~30-40 min

tip.r: Not obligatory but appreciated; 5-10% at restaurants and small tips for guides/drivers are common.

landmarks: The House of Wonders (Beit al-Ajaib)
Once the tallest building in East Africa and the first to have electricity, this grand palace overlooking the harbor is an unmissable symbol of Stone Town's sultanate-era opulence.
Stone Town's Old Fort (Ngome Kongwe)
This imposing 17th-century Omani fortress with crenellated ramparts now hosts craft stalls and cultural performances within its atmospheric coral-stone courtyard.
Forodhani Gardens Night Market
As the sun sets over the harbor, this waterfront park transforms into a sizzling street-food market piled high with Zanzibari pizza, grilled seafood skewers, and sugarcane juice.
Old Slave Market & Anglican Cathedral
Standing on the site of East Africa's largest slave market, this sobering memorial and cathedral confronts Zanzibar's dark history while honoring those who suffered and were freed.
Stone Town's Carved Doors
Wander the labyrinthine alleys to admire hundreds of ornately carved wooden doors studded with brass spikes, each a unique blend of Arab, Indian, and Swahili craftsmanship.
Old Dispensary (Ithnashiri Dispensary)
This exquisitely restored Zanzibari merchant house, with its elaborate carved balconies and stained glass, is one of the most photogenic buildings on the waterfront.
Freddie Mercury's House / Mercury House
A pilgrimage site for music fans, the modest building marking Queen frontman Freddie Mercury's birthplace celebrates the island's most famous son with murals and memorabilia nearby.
Jaws Corner
This lively neighborhood square, named after an old cinema poster, is where locals gather over coffee and gossip — a perfect slice of everyday Stone Town street life.
Prison Island (Changuu) & Giant Tortoises
A short boat ride from Stone Town, this former quarantine island now shelters giant Aldabra tortoises, some over a century old, alongside turquoise snorkeling waters.
Malindi Mosque and Old Dhow Harbour
Watch traditional wooden dhows glide past this historic minaret-topped mosque, a scene that captures centuries of Zanzibar's identity as an Indian Ocean trading crossroads.

train.note: There is no railway on Zanzibar. On the Tanzanian mainland, TRC's new Standard Gauge Railway and the TAZARA line both run from Dar es Salaam, which you reach by ferry (about 2 hours) before boarding a train.

bus.note: Zanzibar is an island, so there are no international or long-distance intercity coaches; getting around is by local dala-dala shared minibuses and taxis. Long-distance mainland buses depart instead from Dar es Salaam, across the channel.

intl.to: Dar es Salaam (Tanzania) - ~2 hr fast catamaran from Stone Town port, with Pemba connections

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international sea route from Zanzibar. Fast catamarans by Azam Marine (Kilimanjaro/Sea Star and Zan Fast) sail several times daily between Zanzibar's Stone Town port and Dar es Salaam (about 2 hours), with connections to Pemba - all domestic Tanzania routes, bookable at azammarine.com. Note that Zanzibar has its own entry formalities, so carry your passport even when arriving from the mainland.
